weeks.context:
AI automation is the practice of combining AI models (language models, vision models, classification models) with workflow orchestration to replace or augment repetitive, judgment-heavy tasks that previously required a human. It is not RPA (Robotic Process Automation) — clicking through UIs with a script — though it can include that. It is not just calling an API and displaying the result. AI automation is building systems that can perceive input, reason about it, act on it, and handle the variation that human workers handle.

The economic model is simple: if a task costs $X per hour and takes Y hours per week, and an AI automation can do it for $0.01 per run in 30 seconds, the business case is obvious. Your job as an AI automation builder is to identify those tasks, build the automations reliably, and deliver them to clients or employers as working systems.

This week you map the landscape: what can AI automation do today (document extraction, classification, drafting, research, data transformation), what it cannot do reliably yet (tasks requiring physical world interaction, novel judgment in high-stakes domains), and what the full toolchain looks like from trigger to output.

mastery_questions: RPA (Robotic Process Automation) is software that mimics a human clicking through a fixed, rules-based process — open this app, copy that field, paste it there — brilliant when the steps never change and the data is structured. AI automation adds a model that can handle the messy, judgment-laden parts RPA chokes on: understanding unstructured text, classifying intent, extracting data from documents that all look different. The dividing line is determinism — RPA needs the world to be predictable; AI automation thrives where it is not. Take invoice processing: if every invoice arrived in the identical template, RPA could scrape it by position, but real invoices come in a thousand layouts, and only a model can read 'the total, wherever it happens to sit'. Give me one task where plain RPA is the right tool, and one where it fails and you genuinely need AI — and name what about the second task breaks the rules-based approach.

The skill here is not listing tasks but recognising the pattern that makes a task a good AI-automation candidate: it is repetitive, high-volume, and involves understanding language or unstructured input that a rigid script cannot handle. Think about where humans currently spend hours doing 'read this, decide, route it' work — triaging support emails into categories, extracting fields from varied invoices or contracts, summarising long documents into a digest, classifying and tagging incoming leads, drafting first-pass replies. In each, a traditional script fails because the input has no fixed structure — the model's ability to generalise across formats is exactly the value. Name five business tasks you would target, and for each one tell me the specific reason a plain if/else script could not do it but a model can.

A trigger is the event that starts an automation — the 'when this happens, do that' clause — and understanding triggers is understanding how automations wake up, because a workflow does nothing until something fires it. The four broad families: a schedule/cron trigger (run every morning at 6am regardless of anything), a webhook trigger (fire instantly when an external system sends an HTTP request — a form submission, a payment), a polling trigger (check a source on an interval — 'any new emails since I last looked?'), and a manual trigger (a human clicks run). Choosing the wrong one shows up as either lag or wasted runs. List four trigger types, and for one of them give me a concrete automation where it is clearly the right choice and a cron trigger would be wrong.

Explaining the economics to a small-business owner is a real skill, because they do not care about LLMs — they care about hours and dollars. The pitch is concrete arithmetic, not technology: 'You pay someone 10 hours a week to copy invoice details into your accounting system — that is roughly so many dollars a year. An automation does it in seconds for a few dollars of API cost a month, frees that person for work that actually grows the business, and does not make tired-Friday-afternoon typos.' You frame it as buying back time and reducing errors, with a payback period they can feel. The trap is overselling perfection — be honest that it needs a human check on edge cases. Give me the exact two-or-three-sentence explanation you would say to a bakery owner who has never heard the term, leading with money, not technology.

This is the question that separates someone who has shipped automation from someone who has only demoed it. LLM-based systems fail in ways scripts do not: they hallucinate (confidently invent a value that was never in the input), they are non-deterministic (the same input can give a slightly different answer), they break on inputs outside what you tested, and they fail silently — returning plausible-looking garbage rather than throwing an error. You build reliability not by hoping the model is perfect but by engineering around its imperfection: validate every output against a schema, add confidence thresholds that route uncertain cases to a human, constrain the model with tool use or structured output, and log everything so you can catch drift. Name the main failure modes, and for hallucination specifically, tell me the concrete control you would put in place so a made-up value never reaches your database.

common_mistakes: Automating the wrong things first — start with tasks that are high-volume, low-variation, and clearly defined. Avoid tasks with high judgment requirements until you have production experience.
Treating LLM output as ground truth without validation — AI automation must include output validation. A model that hallucinates a wrong number in an invoice automation causes real business damage.
Building fragile automations that break on format changes — if your automation parses a specific email format and that format changes, it breaks. Build for variation.
Not considering the error case — every automation must have a fallback: what happens when the LLM returns something unexpected? Log it, alert a human, and don't silently fail.
Overengineering the first version — build the simplest automation that delivers value. Complexity is earned by proved use cases, not anticipated ones.

weeks.title: No-code automation with n8n
weeks.context:
n8n is an open-source workflow automation platform — like Zapier but self-hostable and with a full visual workflow builder. It connects to 400+ services out of the box and lets you write JavaScript in nodes when you need custom logic. For AI automation, n8n is the orchestration layer: it handles the trigger, calls external APIs (including Claude), parses responses, and routes data to the right outputs.

The no-code approach is not a lesser approach — it is faster for many tasks. A workflow that routes incoming Gmail emails based on sentiment, extracts structured data, and adds a row to a Google Sheet should take 20 minutes to build in n8n, not a day in Python. Use the right tool for the complexity of the task.

This week you build 3 complete n8n workflows using Claude: an email classifier that routes support tickets, a document summariser triggered by a webhook, and a daily news digest that pulls from RSS feeds and summarises them.

mastery_questions: In n8n, every workflow is a chain of nodes, and the first distinction to internalise is trigger versus action. A trigger node is the starting block — it does not run as part of a sequence; it listens for an event and kicks off the whole workflow when that event happens (a schedule firing, a webhook receiving a request, a new row appearing). An action node does work once the workflow is already running — it sends an email, calls an API, transforms data, writes to a database. A workflow has exactly one trigger at its head and as many action nodes as the job needs flowing from it. Give me three examples of trigger nodes and three of action nodes, and explain why a workflow cannot start with an action node.

Error handling is where amateur n8n workflows fall apart in production, because by default a node that fails stops the entire workflow dead — and any data still in flight is simply lost. So you have to design for failure deliberately. n8n gives you a few levers: the 'Continue On Fail' setting on a node (let it pass an error downstream instead of halting), a dedicated Error Trigger workflow that runs whenever any workflow errors (to alert you or log it), and retry settings on individual nodes for transient failures. The key mental model: decide, per node, whether a failure should stop everything, be retried, or be caught and routed. Walk me through what happens to the items being processed when a node fails midway, and how you would make sure a single bad record does not kill a batch of a hundred good ones.

n8n passes data between nodes as a list of items, and each node receives the output of the one before it — so the whole system is a pipeline where data flows forward. Inside an expression, $json refers to the data of the current item flowing through the node you are configuring — so $json.email grabs the email field of the item being processed right now. $node lets you reach back and pull data from a specific earlier node by name — for example $node['Webhook'].json.body — which you need when a later node requires a value that an intermediate node dropped. The distinction: $json is 'the thing in front of me', $node is 'go fetch from over there'. Give me an expression using each, and explain a situation where $json is not enough and you must reach back with $node.

Processing 100 emails through an API without getting rate-limited is a real design problem, and the naive approach — fire all 100 at once — gets you throttled or banned. The fix in n8n is to process in controlled batches rather than all-at-once. You use the Split In Batches (Loop Over Items) node to feed items through a few at a time, do the API work inside the loop, and add a Wait node to space out the calls so you stay under the provider's per-minute limit. The mental model is a tap, not a firehose — you deliberately slow the flow to match what the downstream API tolerates. Walk me through structuring that workflow so 100 emails get processed steadily without tripping the rate limit, and tell me where the Wait node goes and why.

This trips people up because both repeat work, but they solve different problems. A regular loop conceptually runs the same step many times, but in n8n's item-based model most nodes already process every item in the input automatically — so you often do not need an explicit loop at all. The Split In Batches node is specifically for chunking a large set of items into smaller groups and processing them group-by-group — essential when you must throttle (rate limits), when downstream can only handle so many at once, or when you want to checkpoint progress through a huge dataset. So: rely on n8n's natural per-item processing for simple transforms; reach for Split In Batches when volume or rate limits force you to control the pace. Tell me a scenario where Split In Batches is necessary and one where it would be needless complexity.

common_mistakes: Not handling rate limits — Claude API has rate limits (requests per minute, tokens per minute). Add a Wait node between batch iterations.
Storing API keys in node configuration instead of environment variables — use n8n credentials or environment variables. Never hardcode keys in workflow nodes.
Not logging intermediate results — when an n8n workflow fails, you need to know which node failed and what data it had. Use Set nodes to capture intermediate state.
Building one huge workflow instead of sub-workflows — n8n supports calling workflows from other workflows. Split complex automations into smaller, testable units.
Not testing with real edge-case data — test with the messiest real emails/documents you have, not clean sample data.

weeks.context:
Python is what you reach for when n8n is not flexible enough. Complex data transformations, custom parsing logic, batch processing at scale, and anything requiring code that reads, writes, or manipulates files is faster and more reliable in Python than in a visual workflow builder.

For AI automation, the Python stack is: httpx or requests for API calls, pydantic for structured output validation, python-dotenv for environment management, schedule or APScheduler for cron-like scheduling, and loguru for structured logging. These five libraries cover 80% of automation scripting tasks.

This week you build automation scripts in Python: a script that monitors a folder for new files and processes them through Claude, a batch email processor, and a data extraction script that reads from a CSV and enriches each row with AI-generated content.

import os

folder = 'test_folder'

mastery_questions: Pydantic is a Python library that lets you define the exact shape your data must take as a class — field names, types, constraints — and then validates real data against it, raising a clear error if anything is wrong. Why does this matter so much for AI automation specifically? Because a model returns text that looks like JSON, but you have no guarantee it included every field, used the right types, or did not hallucinate an extra one — and json.loads() happily parses malformed-but-valid JSON into a dict you then trust blindly. Pydantic turns 'I hope the model returned what I asked for' into 'the model's output is provably the right shape, or my code stops here with a useful error'. It is your contract at the boundary between the unpredictable model and your reliable code. Explain why parsing JSON directly is dangerous for LLM output, and what Pydantic catches that json.loads silently lets through.

When the Anthropic API returns a 500 or 529, it is usually transient — the server was briefly overloaded, and the very same request will likely succeed a moment later — so the correct response is not to crash but to wait and retry. The professional pattern is exponential backoff: retry after 1 second, then 2, then 4, doubling each time (often with a little random jitter so a thousand clients do not all retry in lockstep), giving up after a few attempts. A decorator is the clean way to wrap any API-calling function with this behaviour without cluttering the function itself. The crucial nuance: only retry on transient errors (500, 529, timeouts), never on a 400 — your request is malformed, so retrying just fails again. Sketch a retry decorator with exponential backoff for me, and tell me which error codes you must NOT retry and why.

Synchronous Python does one thing at a time — call the API, sit and wait for the response, then move on — which is simple but wastes enormous time when you are mostly waiting on the network. Asynchronous Python (asyncio) lets your program fire off many API calls and, while waiting for each to come back, work on the others — so 100 calls that each take 2 seconds finish in roughly 2 seconds total instead of 200. The catch: async only helps for I/O-bound work (waiting on network or disk), not CPU-bound work, and it adds real complexity to your code. For AI automation, where you are constantly waiting on API responses, async is often the difference between a job that takes minutes and one that takes hours. Tell me when you would reach for asyncio in an automation and when synchronous code is the right, simpler choice.

Pushing 10,000 files through an AI API is where rate limits become the binding constraint, and the answer combines two ideas: batching and throttling. Throttling means deliberately capping how many requests you send per minute to stay under the provider's limit — you do not get to go as fast as your code can loop. Concurrency control means processing several files in parallel (async) but with a ceiling — a semaphore that allows, say, 5 in flight at once — so you are fast but bounded. You also need durability: checkpoint which files are done so a crash at file 7,000 does not restart you from zero. The mindset is steady, resumable throughput, not raw speed. Describe how you would structure this — the concurrency limit, the throttle, and the checkpointing — and explain what a semaphore is actually doing in that design.

The watchdog library lets Python react to filesystem events — a file created, modified, moved, or deleted in a folder you are watching — rather than you repeatedly checking 'anything new yet?'. This turns a polling problem into an event-driven one: instead of a script that wakes every 30 seconds to scan a directory (wasteful, and laggy), watchdog calls your handler the instant a file lands. For automation, this is the backbone of 'drop a file in this folder and it gets processed automatically' — an invoice lands, watchdog fires, your pipeline runs. The benefit over polling is immediacy and efficiency. weeks.title: Calling AI APIs
weeks.context:
Every major AI model is available via an API. Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT-4, o1), Google (Gemini), Mistral, Cohere, Together AI — each has a REST API and a Python SDK. This week you learn to call them effectively: structured outputs, tool use / function calling, streaming, and multi-turn conversations.

Structured outputs are how you make AI automation reliable. Instead of asking the model to "return JSON", you define a schema and force the model to return data that matches it. Claude has tool use / JSON mode; OpenAI has structured outputs. When the model is constrained to a schema, parsing errors drop to near zero.

Tool use (also called function calling) is the mechanism that enables agents: you describe a set of tools the model can call (search the web, query a database, send an email), the model decides which tool to call and with what arguments, your code executes the tool, and you return the result to the model. This loop is the foundation of autonomous AI agents.

from openai import OpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

    r = client.chat.completions.create(

summary = summarise(message)

mastery_questions: Both JSON mode and tool use get structured data out of a model, but they work differently and tool use is often the better choice even when you are 'just extracting'. JSON mode simply constrains the model to return valid JSON text — useful, but the structure is only as disciplined as your prompt. Tool use defines a tool with an explicit input schema (the exact fields and types you want), and the model fills that schema as if calling a function — so the structure is enforced by the schema, not just requested in prose. Even for simple extraction, tool use gives you a guaranteed shape and types, which is why it is more reliable than asking for JSON in the prompt and hoping. Explain the difference, and tell me why you might reach for tool use to extract a single name-and-date pair rather than just asking for JSON.

The tool use loop is the heartbeat of every agent, so understand it precisely. You send the model a message plus the tools it is allowed to use. The model does not execute anything itself — instead it can respond with a 'tool_use' block saying, in effect, 'call get_weather with city=Paris'. Your code sees that, actually runs get_weather, and sends the result back to the model as a 'tool_result' message. The model then continues — it might answer the user, or call another tool, and the loop repeats until it produces a final text answer. The key insight beginners miss: the model only decides and requests; your code does the doing. Walk me through one full cycle — model decides, your code executes, result goes back — and explain whose responsibility it is to actually run the tool.

Streaming means the API sends the response token-by-token as the model generates it, rather than making you wait for the entire completion before you see anything. For user-facing automations this is the difference between a chatbot that feels alive — words appearing as you watch — and one that sits frozen for ten seconds before dumping a wall of text. A regular blocking call returns the whole response at once: simpler to code, fine for back-end batch jobs where no human is watching, but painful when a person is waiting on the other end. The trade-off is purely about perceived latency and user experience, not total speed. Tell me when streaming genuinely matters and when a blocking call is perfectly fine, and explain why a nightly batch job has no need for it.

A multi-turn conversation in the Anthropic API works because the API itself is stateless — it does not remember anything between calls. You create the illusion of memory by sending the entire conversation history back with every request, as an ever-growing messages array that alternates user and assistant roles. After three turns it looks like: user, assistant, user, assistant, user, assistant — each new user message appended to the full prior list, and you resend the whole thing. The model reads the accumulated history as context and replies in character. The consequence beginners miss: the conversation grows every turn, costing more tokens, so long chats eventually need trimming or summarising. Show me what the messages array looks like after three turns, and explain why you must resend the whole history rather than just the latest message.

Choosing a model is an engineering trade-off between intelligence, speed, and cost, and a good automation builder picks deliberately rather than defaulting to the biggest. Roughly: Haiku is the fastest and cheapest, ideal for high-volume, well-defined tasks like classification or simple extraction where you are doing the same easy thing thousands of times. Sonnet is the balanced workhorse — strong reasoning at reasonable cost and speed — the default for most real automation work. Opus is the most capable for genuinely hard reasoning, complex multi-step judgment, or tricky edge cases, at higher cost and latency. The skill is matching model to task: do not pay top-tier prices to sort emails into three buckets. Give me one automation task suited to each tier, and explain the cost-versus-capability reasoning that drives your choice.

weeks.title: Prompt engineering for automation
weeks.context:
Prompt engineering for automation is different from prompt engineering for chat. In a chat context, you iterate in real time and adjust. In automation, the prompt runs thousands of times without you watching. A prompt that works 95% of the time has a 5% failure rate — at 1,000 runs per day, that is 50 failures per day.

Reliability is the primary metric for automation prompts. A prompt that extracts data correctly 95% of the time at scale is worse than a prompt that achieves 99.9% — because at scale, 5% failures are operational incidents. This week you learn the techniques that move prompts from "usually works" to "always works": few-shot examples, explicit output constraints, chain-of-thought for complex tasks, and systematic prompt testing.

You also learn to write system prompts that are robust: they define the task, the constraints, the output format, how to handle uncertainty, and what to do when the input is ambiguous or missing required information.

mastery_questions: A few-shot example is a worked example you put right in the prompt — here is an input, and here is exactly the output I want for it — usually a few of them, before the real input. They improve extraction accuracy more than piling on instructions because models learn far better from demonstration than description: 'extract the date in ISO format' is an instruction the model might interpret loosely, but showing it three inputs each paired with a 2024-03-15 style output makes the target unambiguous. Examples also pin down edge cases that prose struggles to specify — how to handle a missing field, an ambiguous format. The lesson: when accuracy matters, show, do not just tell. Explain why two or three examples often beat a paragraph of extra instructions, and give me a case where a few-shot example fixes an ambiguity that instructions alone could not.

A prompt that fails on 5% of inputs is a debugging problem, and the amateur move is to randomly tweak wording and hope. The systematic process: first, collect the failures — log every input and output so you actually have the 5% in front of you, rather than guessing. Second, categorise them — are they all the same kind of input (a format you did not anticipate, a missing field, an unusually long document)? Failures usually cluster. Third, form a hypothesis about the cause and add a targeted few-shot example or instruction addressing that exact category. Fourth, re-run against your whole test set, including the previously-passing 95%, to confirm you fixed the failures without breaking the wins. It is the scientific method, not vibes. Walk me through how you would go from '5% fail' to a fix, and stress why you must re-test the 95% that already worked.

Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before giving its answer, rather than jumping straight to a conclusion — and it genuinely improves accuracy on tasks that require multi-step reasoning (math, logic, complex classification with rules) because the model works it out instead of guessing. But it is not free: all that reasoning is extra tokens, which means more latency and more cost on every single call. For a high-volume automation doing simple extraction, forcing chain-of-thought on every run can double your latency for no accuracy gain. The judgment is matching it to task difficulty. Tell me a task where chain-of-thought clearly helps and one where it just adds latency, and explain how you would get the reasoning benefit without paying the token cost on the simple cases.

Getting a model to return null for a missing field instead of inventing one is a critical reliability technique, because a hallucinated value is far more dangerous than an honest blank — it looks real and slips into your database undetected. Models have a strong instinct to be 'helpful' and fill in an answer, so you must explicitly give them permission and instruction to abstain: state clearly that if a field is not present in the input they must return null (or a defined empty value), and reinforce it with a few-shot example showing an input missing that field paired with a null output. Structured output via tool use, with the field marked optional, helps enforce it. The core idea: you have to make 'I don't know' an allowed, demonstrated answer. Tell me how you would instruct and demonstrate this, and why a hallucinated phone number is worse than a blank one.

Temperature controls how random the model's output is — low temperature makes it pick the most probable next token almost every time (consistent, predictable), high temperature lets it take less likely paths (varied, creative). For extraction and classification you want temperature near 0, and the reasoning is simple: these tasks have a single correct answer, and you want the same input to give the same output every time — randomness here is just a source of bugs and irreproducibility. You save higher temperatures for genuinely generative tasks where variety is the point — drafting marketing copy, brainstorming names. The principle: deterministic tasks want deterministic settings. Explain what temperature actually changes in the model's choices, and tell me why a temperature of 0.9 would be a mistake for an invoice-field extractor.

**Prompt testing framework:**
```python
import json
from anthropic import Anthropic
from typing import Callable

client = Anthropic()

def test_prompt(
    system_prompt: str,
    test_cases: list[dict],
    evaluator: Callable,
    model: str = "claude-3-5-haiku-20241022"
) -> dict:
    results = []
    for case in test_cases:
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=model,
            max_tokens=500,
            system=system_prompt,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["input"]}]
        )
        output = response.content[0].text
        passed = evaluator(output, case["expected"])
        results.append({"input": case["input"], "output": output, "passed": passed})

    pass_rate = sum(r["passed"] for r in results) / len(results)
    return {"pass_rate": pass_rate, "results": results}
```

weeks.title: AI agents — what they are and how they work

resources.label: OpenAI function calling docs
resources.note: The technical foundation of most agents

weeks.context:
An AI agent is an LLM in a loop. The model receives a task, decides on an action, your code executes that action, the result comes back to the model, and the loop continues until the model decides the task is complete. The key insight: the model is the reasoner, your code is the executor.

The ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) pattern is the foundation of most agent architectures: the model outputs a Thought (what it is trying to do), an Action (which tool to call with which arguments), and after you execute the action, an Observation (the result). This repeats until the model outputs a Final Answer.

Understanding agents at this level — not as magic, but as a specific loop with specific failure modes — is what separates builders who can debug and improve agents from users who can only run pre-built ones.

items.title: Add a reasoning step
items.body:
Modify your system prompt to:

'You are a helpful assistant with access to tools. Before calling any tool, explain in one sentence WHY you are calling it. Format your reasoning as: [REASON: ...] then proceed.'

Ask a multi-step question like: 'What is the weather in the capital of France?'

The agent should:
1. Reason that it needs to know France's capital → call search_web('capital of France')
2. Get 'Paris' back
3. Then call get_weather('Paris')

This is the ReAct pattern — the foundation of most production agents.

mastery_questions: The ReAct pattern (Reasoning + Acting) is the loop that makes an agent more than a single API call, and its three beats always occur in the same order. Thought: the model reasons about what it needs to do next ('to answer this, I should search for the latest price'). Action: it takes a step in the world by calling a tool ('search("current gold price")'). Observation: it receives the tool's result back ('gold is $2,400/oz') and feeds that into its next Thought. Then it loops — Thought, Action, Observation — accumulating knowledge until it has enough to give a final answer. The power is that the model's reasoning is interleaved with real-world feedback instead of guessing in one shot. Walk me through a ReAct cycle for 'what is the weather in the capital of France', naming each Thought, Action, and Observation in order.

In the Anthropic API, 'tool call' and 'function call' refer to essentially the same mechanism — you define a capability with a schema, and the model requests that it be invoked with specific arguments — and the terminology difference is mostly historical (other providers popularised 'function calling'; Anthropic's API uses 'tool use'). What matters is not the word but the discipline behind it: you describe the tool, its purpose, and its input schema clearly enough that the model knows when and how to use it, and your code remains responsible for actually executing it and returning the result. Confusing the names costs nothing; confusing who runs the tool costs you a broken agent. Confirm whether they are the same thing in the Anthropic API, and explain the one responsibility that stays with your code regardless of what the mechanism is called.

When an agent calls a tool that returns an error, the worst thing you can do is crash the loop — because handling failure gracefully is exactly what makes an agent robust. Instead of throwing, you feed the error back to the model as the tool result: 'the search failed with a timeout' or 'no file found at that path'. This is powerful because a capable model can then reason about the failure and recover — retry with different arguments, try an alternative tool, or tell the user it cannot complete the task. The agent gets a chance to adapt, just as a human would when a first attempt fails. The anti-pattern is swallowing the error silently, which leaves the model blind. Tell me how you would return a tool error to the model, and what good recovery behaviour looks like versus a silent failure.

A max_iterations limit caps how many times the agent loop can run before you force it to stop, and it exists to prevent the most common and expensive agent failure: the infinite loop. Without it, an agent that gets confused can call the same tool over and over, or bounce between two actions forever, burning API tokens (real money) and never terminating — a runaway you might not notice until the bill arrives. The limit is a circuit breaker: after, say, 10 iterations, you stop and return whatever you have, or escalate to a human. It does not fix the underlying confusion, but it bounds the damage. Explain the specific failure mode max_iterations prevents, and tell me what you would do when an agent hits the limit rather than just silently stopping.

A chain is a fixed, predetermined sequence of steps — do A, then B, then C, every time, in the same order — while an agent decides its own steps dynamically, choosing which tools to call and when based on what it observes. The crucial judgment is not to reach for an agent when a chain will do, because agents are more powerful but also less predictable, slower, and harder to debug. If your task always follows the same path — extract fields, validate, write to database — a chain is simpler, cheaper, and more reliable. You need an agent only when the path genuinely cannot be known in advance, because it depends on what the model discovers along the way. Give me one task best solved by a simple chain and one that truly requires an agent, and explain what makes the second one impossible to hard-code as a chain.
common_mistakes: Not limiting tool execution — an agent can call tools in an infinite loop. Always set a max_iterations limit and log how many iterations a task uses.
Giving the agent too many tools — models perform better with fewer, well-defined tools. More than 10 tools in a single agent degrades performance.
Using eval() for calculations without sandboxing — in production, never use eval() on user input. Use a proper math expression parser library.
Not including tool error handling in the agent loop — if a tool raises an exception, the agent should receive an error message, not a crash.
Building an agent for a task that a simple prompt solves — if the task has a fixed set of steps, use a chain, not an agent. Agents add complexity and cost.

weeks.context:
Web scraping plus AI is more powerful than either alone. Traditional scraping uses CSS selectors or XPath — brittle, breaks when the page changes. AI-powered scraping uses the model to extract structured data from raw HTML or text, making the extraction logic robust to layout changes.

The workflow: fetch the page (requests + BeautifulSoup for static pages, Playwright for JavaScript-rendered pages), convert HTML to markdown or plain text to reduce token count, send to Claude with an extraction prompt, parse the structured output. Ethical and legal note: always check robots.txt before scraping, respect rate limits (1-2 requests per second maximum for well-behaved scrapers), and do not scrape personal data without a legal basis. Many websites have terms of service that prohibit scraping — read them first.

mastery_questions: requests + BeautifulSoup and Playwright solve web scraping at two different layers, and using the heavier tool when you do not need it just makes your scraper slow and fragile. requests fetches the raw HTML a server sends, and BeautifulSoup parses it — fast, lightweight, perfect when the content you want is already in that initial HTML. But many modern sites send a near-empty HTML shell and then build the page with JavaScript in the browser — and requests never runs JavaScript, so the data simply is not there. That is when you need Playwright: it drives a real browser, executes the JavaScript, waits for content to render, and can click and scroll like a user. The rule: requests for static HTML, Playwright when the content only appears after JavaScript runs. Tell me how you would detect that a site needs Playwright, and the cost you pay for using it unnecessarily.

Converting HTML to markdown before sending it to Claude is a token-economics decision, and it can dramatically cut your costs. Raw HTML is bloated with tags, attributes, inline styles, scripts, and navigation chrome — a single article page can be tens of thousands of tokens of mostly noise that the model has to read (and you have to pay for). Markdown strips all that down to the actual content and its structure (headings, lists, links) in a fraction of the tokens — often a large reduction — while preserving everything the model needs to understand the page. Fewer tokens means lower cost, faster responses, and more room in the context window. Explain why raw HTML is so token-expensive compared to markdown, and roughly what kind of token reduction you would expect from stripping a content page down.

robots.txt is a file at the root of a website that tells automated crawlers which paths the site owner asks them not to access — it is a stated convention, the web's 'please do not enter' sign. A line like 'Disallow: /api/' means the owner is requesting that crawlers not hit anything under the /api/ path. The important nuances: it is advisory, not a technical lock (your code can ignore it, but doing so can be a legal and ethical problem and a fast route to an IP ban), and respecting it is part of being a responsible scraper. Treat it as the first thing you read before scraping a site. Explain what 'Disallow: /api/' is asking of you, and tell me why ignoring robots.txt is risky even though nothing technically stops you.

Rate limiting your own scraper is about being a polite, sustainable guest rather than hammering a server until it blocks you — because aggressive scraping gets your IP banned and can degrade the site for real users. The core technique is to deliberately space out your requests: add a delay between them (and ideally a randomised delay, so your pattern looks less like a machine), limit concurrency so you are not firing dozens at once, and respect any Retry-After headers the server sends when it is overloaded. The goal is to stay under the threshold that triggers defensive blocking. Describe how you would pace a scraper across a few hundred pages to avoid a ban, and explain why a randomised delay is better than a fixed one.

CSS selectors and XPath are two languages for pointing at elements in an HTML document, and while CSS selectors handle the vast majority of cases cleanly, XPath can express things CSS cannot. CSS selectors target elements by tag, class, id, and hierarchy — '.price', 'div.product > span' — and are concise and readable. XPath navigates the document tree more powerfully: it can select an element based on its text content, traverse upward to a parent or ancestor, or pick the element that follows another — none of which CSS selectors can do directly. The classic example: 'find the price that comes right after the label that says Total' requires XPath's text-matching and axis navigation. Give me an example where XPath is genuinely more powerful than a CSS selector, and explain what CSS structurally cannot do that XPath can.

**Pattern 1 — Static page scraping + AI extraction:**
```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from markdownify import markdownify as md
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def scrape_and_extract(url: str, extraction_prompt: str) -> dict:
    # Fetch page
    response = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"})
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")

    # Remove nav, footer, scripts (reduce noise)
    for tag in soup.find_all(["nav", "footer", "script", "style", "aside"]):
        tag.decompose()

    # Convert to markdown (much shorter than raw HTML)
    text = md(str(soup.body), strip=["img", "a"])[:8000]  # limit tokens

    # Extract with Claude
    message = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-haiku-20241022",
        max_tokens=1000,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"{extraction_prompt}\n\nContent:\n{text}"
        }]
    )
    return message.content[0].text
```

**Pattern 2 — JavaScript-rendered pages with Playwright:**
```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

def scrape_dynamic(url: str) -> str:
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        browser = p.chromium.launch()
        page = browser.new_page()
        page.goto(url)
        page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")
        content = page.content()
        browser.close()
    return content
```

Not rotating User-Agent headers — many sites block default Python/requests User-Agent strings. Use a realistic browser User-Agent.
No delay between requests — scraping at full speed will trigger rate limiting or IP bans. Add random sleep between requests: time.sleep(random.uniform(1, 3)).
Not handling 403/429 responses — check the status code before parsing the response body. A 403 HTML page looks like content but is an access denied page.

mastery_questions: Text-based and vision-based PDF extraction suit two different kinds of document, and choosing wrong either wastes money or misses data entirely. Text-based extraction (pdfplumber and friends) pulls the actual text layer out of a PDF — fast, cheap, exact — and it works whenever the PDF genuinely contains selectable text. But it falls apart on scanned documents (a photo of a page has no text layer, just pixels) and on complex layouts where reading order and tables get scrambled. Vision-based extraction sends the page as an image to Claude, which reads it the way a human looks at it — handling scans, stamps, handwriting, and messy layouts — at higher cost and latency. The rule: text extraction for clean digital PDFs, vision for scans and visually complex pages. Tell me how you would decide which to use on a given PDF, and what specifically text extraction fails on that vision handles.

A 50-page contract against a context window that holds 15 pages is a classic chunking problem, and the naive 'just send it all' simply will not fit. The strategy is to split the document into overlapping chunks that each fit comfortably in the window, process them, and then combine. The detail that matters: you overlap the chunks slightly (a few hundred tokens shared between consecutive chunks) so that a clause spanning a chunk boundary is not cut in half and lost. For extraction you might run each chunk and merge results; for a question you might retrieve only the relevant chunks (RAG) rather than reading all of them. The art is splitting on natural boundaries (sections, clauses) rather than mid-sentence. Describe your chunking strategy for the 50-page contract, and explain why overlap between chunks matters.

OCR (Optical Character Recognition) is the technology that turns an image of text — a scanned page, a photo of a receipt — into actual machine-readable characters, and it is needed precisely when a document has no text layer, only pixels. Traditional OCR (like Tesseract) is a separate, often finicky step: it can struggle with poor scans, unusual fonts, tables, and layout, and it hands you raw text with no understanding of meaning. Claude's vision capability collapses this into one step — it reads the image and extracts the structured information you actually want, in context, often handling messy scans and layouts that trip up classic OCR, without a separate OCR pipeline. Explain when OCR is needed at all, and how sending the page to Claude's vision reduces your reliance on a traditional OCR step.

Validating extracted data is the difference between an invoice pipeline you can trust unattended and one that quietly corrupts your books. Because the model can misread or hallucinate, every extraction needs automated checks before the data is accepted: type and format checks (is the date a real date, the total a number?), arithmetic checks (do the line items sum to the stated subtotal, and subtotal plus tax equal the total?), business-rule checks (is the date plausible, the vendor known, the amount within an expected range?), and a confidence or completeness check (are required fields present, or should this go to a human?). The arithmetic cross-check is especially powerful because it catches a misread digit that looks perfectly valid on its own. List the checks you would run on every invoice extraction, and explain why the line-items-sum-to-total check catches errors a format check never would.

An end-to-end invoice pipeline is a great integration exercise, so trace it from trigger to stored row. It starts with a trigger — an invoice arrives as an email attachment, which a watcher or webhook detects. The attachment is pulled and its type checked; if it is a clean digital PDF you extract text, if it is a scan you send the page image to Claude's vision. The model extracts the fields into a structured schema (vendor, date, line items, totals), enforced with something like Pydantic. Then validation runs — the arithmetic and format checks — and anything that fails or scores low confidence is routed to a human for review rather than written blindly. Finally the validated record is written to the database, and the source file archived. Walk me through that pipeline stage by stage, and tell me which stage you would never let run without a human fallback, and why.

weeks.context:
Email is the highest-volume communication channel in most businesses, and it is a goldmine for AI automation. Classifying incoming emails, drafting responses, extracting action items, routing support tickets, and generating personalised outreach at scale — all of these are tractable AI automation problems.

The key to reliable email automation is the human-in-the-loop design pattern: the AI drafts or suggests, a human reviews before sending. Fully autonomous email sending is appropriate only for narrow, well-tested cases (like confirmation emails from structured triggers). For anything involving judgment about what to say to a human, keep a human in the loop.

This week you build three email automations: an inbox classifier that labels and routes incoming email, a response drafter that generates suggested replies for support emails, and a personalised outreach generator that creates unique emails from a prospect list.

mastery_questions: The Gmail API scopes 'gmail.readonly' and 'gmail.modify' encode a security principle you should apply everywhere: grant only the permission the job actually needs. 'gmail.readonly' lets your automation read messages but change nothing — perfect for a classifier or a digest builder that only needs to look. 'gmail.modify' additionally lets it change mailbox state — add or remove labels, mark as read, move messages — which you need only when the automation must act on the inbox, not just observe it. Asking for modify when you only read is over-privileged: if your credentials leak, the attacker can alter the user's mail. The lesson is least privilege — request the narrowest scope that does the job. Tell me which scope a support-email classifier that only sorts and reports needs, and when you would be justified in stepping up to modify.

Designing an email classification system for a SaaS support inbox is really about defining categories that map to actions, not just topics — a label is useless unless it changes what happens next. Sensible categories might be: billing question, bug report, feature request, account/login issue, and general/other — each routing to a different team or workflow. The hard part is the ambiguous email that fits two categories or none, and a robust design plans for it explicitly: have the model return a confidence level, route low-confidence or multi-category messages to a human triage queue rather than forcing a guess, and allow a fallback 'needs human' label. Designing for the ambiguous case is what keeps the system from confidently misrouting. Define your categories, and tell me exactly how you would handle an email the model is unsure about instead of forcing it into a bucket.

Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or approves the automation's output before it takes an irreversible action — and for email it is the line between a helpful assistant and an embarrassing disaster. The pattern: the automation drafts the reply or classification, but a human approves before anything is sent to a customer. You can safely fully automate the low-risk, reversible, or internal actions — labelling, sorting, drafting, sending an internal notification — because a mistake there is cheap to undo. You keep a human in the loop for anything customer-facing or irreversible, especially early on, because a wrongly-sent email cannot be unsent and damages trust. The judgment is calibrating autonomy to the cost of being wrong. Tell me which email actions you would fully automate and which require approval, and the principle that decides each.

Personalising outreach at scale without it feeling templated is a genuine craft, because the moment a recipient senses a mail-merge, your credibility evaporates. The weak approach swaps in a first name and a company name into a fixed template — recipients see straight through it. Real personalisation uses specifics that prove you (or your automation) actually looked: referencing something concrete about their company, a recent announcement, a detail from their site — generated per-recipient by the model from researched data, not slotted into a rigid frame. The model writes a genuinely tailored sentence or two, while you keep the ask consistent. The balance is scale with specificity, and honesty about it. Tell me what makes a personalised email feel genuine versus templated, and one concrete signal you would have the model incorporate per recipient.

Automated outreach is regulated, and ignorance is not a defence — both the US (CAN-SPAM) and the EU (GDPR plus the ePrivacy rules) impose real requirements, with the EU being notably stricter. Broadly, every commercial email must include a clear way to unsubscribe (and you must honour it promptly), a valid physical postal address, honest non-deceptive subject lines and sender information, and identification as a commercial message. The big EU difference is consent: GDPR generally requires a lawful basis — often prior opt-in consent — to email individuals, whereas the US model is more opt-out (you may email until they unsubscribe, within rules). Getting this wrong risks fines and blacklisting. Tell me what every marketing email must include regardless of region, and the key consent difference between emailing into the EU versus the US.

weeks.context:
Databases and spreadsheets hold the structured data that drives business decisions. AI automation connects these data stores to intelligence: generating SQL from natural language, enriching database rows with AI-generated content, building automated reporting pipelines, and creating smart spreadsheet functions.

Natural language to SQL (text-to-SQL) is one of the most valuable enterprise automation patterns. Instead of requiring a data analyst to write SQL for every ad-hoc question, you build a system where business users ask questions in plain English and get SQL-generated answers. The key to making this reliable: the model needs your database schema, table descriptions, and example queries as context.

This week you build a natural language query interface for a SQLite database, an automated data enrichment pipeline, and a Google Sheets automation that uses the Sheets API + Claude to add AI-generated columns.

mastery_questions: You must include the database schema in a text-to-SQL prompt because the model cannot query what it cannot see — without the table and column names, types, and relationships, it is forced to guess. And a guessing model does not fail loudly; it invents plausible-sounding table and column names ('users.signup_date' when your column is actually 'created_at'), producing SQL that looks correct but errors out or, worse, runs against the wrong columns and returns confidently wrong numbers. Giving it the schema — tables, columns, types, and key relationships — grounds it in your actual database so it generates valid, correct queries. The schema is the map; without it the model is navigating blind. Explain what specifically goes wrong when you omit the schema, and why a hallucinated column name can be more dangerous than an outright error.

Letting an AI-generated SQL query touch your database unguarded is one of the riskiest things in automation, so you layer safety measures before execution. First, restrict to read-only: the database user the automation connects as should have SELECT privileges only, so even a malicious or buggy query physically cannot DROP, DELETE, or UPDATE anything. Second, validate the generated SQL — confirm it is a SELECT, reject anything containing destructive statements, and ideally parse it rather than string-matching. Third, bound it — add a LIMIT, set a query timeout, run against a replica if possible — so a runaway query cannot exhaust the database. Defence in depth means even if one check fails, the read-only user saves you. List the safety measures you would apply, and explain why the read-only database user is the most important single control.

A text-to-SQL system that generates a query which is syntactically perfect and runs cleanly but answers the wrong question is the most insidious failure, because nothing errors — you just get confident, wrong numbers. The model might join the wrong tables, misinterpret 'active users' (active how? in what window?), or apply a filter you did not intend, and the result looks authoritative. The defences are about catching semantic drift: show the user the generated SQL and a plain-English restatement of what it does before trusting the result, validate the output against a sanity range or a known-answer test, and design prompts that force the model to state its assumptions. You cannot fully automate trust here — you build in verification. Tell me how you would detect a semantically-wrong-but-valid query, and why this failure is more dangerous than a syntax error.

The Google Sheets API offers two auth models, and the right one depends on whose data you are touching. A service account is a non-human identity — a robot account with its own credentials — that you grant access to specific sheets; it is ideal for server-side automation that runs unattended and acts as itself, with no user present to log in. OAuth (user authorisation) has the automation act on behalf of a specific human user who logs in and consents, getting access to that user's own files; it is what you use when the automation needs to read or write sheets owned by the end user, not by your service. The rule: service account for your own backend automation, OAuth when acting as a specific user on their data. Tell me which you would use for a nightly job writing to a company-owned reporting sheet, and which for a tool that edits each user's personal sheets.

A data enrichment pipeline takes thin records and uses the model to add inferred fields, and a customer table with just name and company is a perfect case — but it is also where hallucination risk is highest, so design accordingly. The flow: for each row, you prompt Claude with the name and company to infer industry, an estimated company size band, and a likely job title, returning a structured, validated schema. The critical discipline is treating these as estimates, not facts: instruct the model to return null when it genuinely cannot infer rather than guessing, attach a confidence level, and never present an inferred job title as confirmed truth. You might also ground it with a real data source (a company lookup) rather than pure inference. Walk me through the pipeline, and tell me how you would stop the model from confidently inventing an industry for a company it knows nothing about.

```python
def get_schema(db_path: str) -> str:

    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute("SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'")
    schemas = cursor.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return "\n".join(s[0] for s in schemas if s[0])

def natural_language_to_sql(question: str, db_path: str) -> str:
    schema = get_schema(db_path)
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022",
        max_tokens=500,
        system=f"""You are a SQL expert. Generate SQLite SQL queries from natural language questions.
Database schema:
{schema}

Rules:
- Return ONLY the SQL query, no explanation
- Use SQLite syntax
- Never use destructive operations (DROP, DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT)
- If the question cannot be answered from the schema, return: SELECT 'Cannot answer: [reason]'""",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}]
    )
    return response.content[0].text.strip()

def run_query(question: str, db_path: str) -> list[dict]:
    sql = natural_language_to_sql(question, db_path)
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    try:
        cursor.execute(sql)
        return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
    except Exception as e:
        return [{"error": str(e), "sql": sql}]
    finally:
        conn.close()
```

weeks.title: LangChain basics
weeks.context:
LangChain is a framework for building LLM-powered applications. It provides abstractions for the most common patterns: chains (sequences of LLM calls), agents (LLMs with tools), memory (persisting conversation state), and document loaders + retrievers (for RAG). The value of LangChain is reducing boilerplate — the same patterns you would implement manually in 200 lines take 20 lines with LangChain.

The critique of LangChain is equally valid: it adds abstraction and magic that makes debugging harder, and its API surface changes frequently. For production systems, many teams drop LangChain and implement the specific patterns they need directly. You should know both approaches: LangChain for rapid prototyping and experimentation, direct API calls for production.

This week you use LangChain to build the same automations you built in Python in previous weeks — compare the implementation and form your own opinion.

items.title: Two-step research chain
items.body:
Create sequential_chain.py:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')
parser = StrOutputParser()

# Step 1: generate outline
outline_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('system', 'Generate a 3-point outline for a blog post on this topic. Be concise.'),
    ('user', '{topic}')
])

# Step 2: write intro from outline
intro_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('system', 'Write a punchy 2-sentence blog intro based on this outline.'),
    ('user', '{outline}')
])

# Chain them
outline_chain = outline_prompt | llm | parser
intro_chain = intro_prompt | llm | parser

full_chain = outline_chain | (lambda outline: {'outline': outline}) | intro_chain

result = full_chain.invoke({'topic': 'AI automation for small businesses in Africa'})
print(result)

mastery_questions: LangChain is a framework that lets you wire AI components together like plumbing, and its core trick is LCEL — the LangChain Expression Language. In LCEL you connect pieces using the pipe operator, the same vertical bar you see in a Unix shell, so 'prompt | model | parser' means the output of the prompt feeds the model, and the model's output feeds the parser. The reason this matters is that each piece becomes swappable and the whole chain gets streaming and async behaviour for free. Picture a chain that takes a user's product review, formats it into a prompt asking for sentiment, sends it to Claude, then parses the reply into clean text. Walk me through that chain piece by piece, and tell me what each '|' is actually passing to the next stage.

There is a distinction in LangChain that trips up almost everyone, so let's nail it. A chain is a fixed sequence of steps you decided in advance — step one always feeds step two, like a recipe. An agent is different: you hand the model a set of tools and let IT decide which tool to call and in what order, looping until it thinks the job is done. The rule of thumb is use a chain when you know the steps ahead of time, and use an agent only when the path genuinely depends on what the model discovers along the way, because agents are slower, costlier, and harder to debug. Give me one task from your own work that should be a chain, and one that truly needs an agent, and defend why each can't be the other.

When an LLM app misbehaves in production, the worst feeling is not knowing what actually happened inside the chain. LangSmith is LangChain's observability tool — it records a trace of every run, meaning the exact prompt sent, the raw model response, token counts, latency, and which step failed. Think of it as a flight recorder for your chain: when a customer says 'the bot gave me a wrong answer', you open the trace and see the precise inputs and outputs at each stage instead of guessing. Explain to me what you would look for in a LangSmith trace if your summarization chain suddenly started returning empty strings.

LangChain is popular but it has loud critics, and a good engineer can argue both sides. The main complaint is that its abstractions hide too much — when something breaks, you are debugging LangChain's internals instead of your own logic, and a simple task can become a tangle of wrappers. For a lot of production work, a few direct API calls with your own code are clearer, faster, and easier to maintain than pulling in the whole framework. So here's the judgement call I want from you: describe a project where LangChain genuinely earns its place, and a different one where you would skip it and just call the API directly — and tell me what tips the decision.

Models return raw text, but your code usually needs structured data, and that gap is what output parsers close. StrOutputParser simply takes the model's reply and hands you back a clean string — use it when you just want the words, like a chatbot answer. JsonOutputParser expects the model to return JSON and gives you back a parsed object with real fields you can access, like result['category'] — use it when downstream code needs to branch on specific values. The catch is that models sometimes return slightly malformed JSON, so the JSON parser is doing real work to coax and validate that structure. Walk me through a classification automation where you'd reach for JsonOutputParser, and tell me what breaks if you'd used StrOutputParser instead.

weeks.context:
An autonomous agent operates without human intervention from start to finish on multi-step tasks. This week you build one that is genuinely useful: a research agent that takes a topic, searches the web, reads the most relevant pages, synthesises the information, and writes a structured research report.

The architecture: a ReAct loop with 3 tools (web search, page reader, write-report), a system prompt that defines the research process and output format, and a stopping condition when the model decides it has enough information. The challenge is reliability — agents fail in unpredictable ways, and you need to build monitoring and guardrails from the start.

You also learn the concept of agent evaluation: how do you measure whether an agent is doing a good job? You build a small test harness that runs the agent on 5 known tasks and scores the output quality.

items.body:
Run your research agent on 3 topics:
1. 'AI automation trends in Africa 2026'
2. 'Python web scraping best practices'
3. 'How to price freelance automation services'

For each run, note:
- How many steps did the agent take?
- Did it save the file correctly?
- Was the report accurate?
- Did it loop or get confused anywhere?

Write a short 'agent evaluation' doc. This is how you improve agents in production.

mastery_questions: An autonomous agent that researches a topic faces one dangerous question: when do I stop? Without a clear stopping condition it will keep searching forever, burning tokens and money. The clean way to handle this is to give the agent an explicit goal and a 'finish' tool it calls when it believes the goal is met — for example, the agent keeps gathering sources until it can answer all the sub-questions it was asked, then it calls finish and writes the report. You also set a hard ceiling, a max number of steps, as a safety net in case its judgement fails. Walk me through the stopping logic for a research agent investigating 'best CRM for a 5-person agency', and tell me both the natural finish signal and the hard backstop you'd set.

Research agents have a nasty habit: they get stuck rerunning the same search query over and over, convinced they need more data. The fix is to give the agent memory of what it has already tried — you keep a record of past queries and results in its context, and instruct it not to repeat a search it has already run. A stronger version dedupes queries programmatically before they execute, so an identical search is simply blocked and the agent is nudged to try a different angle. Tell me how you'd detect that an agent is looping on duplicate queries just by reading its trace, and what you'd change to break the loop.

You can't improve an agent you can't measure, so let's talk agent evaluation — judging the quality of an agent's output systematically rather than eyeballing it. For a research agent you might score each run on whether it answered every sub-question, whether its claims are backed by the sources it cited, and whether it avoided contradicting itself. A practical setup is a fixed test set of research tasks with known good answers, run the agent against them, and have a stronger model or a rubric grade the outputs so you get a repeatable score. Describe how you'd build a small eval set for a research agent and what three things you'd grade each run on.

Every agent type fails in its own characteristic ways, and knowing them is half the battle. For a research agent, three classic failure modes are: hallucinated sources where it cites pages that don't exist or don't say what it claims; premature finishing where it stops before actually covering the question; and tunnel vision where it fixates on one angle and ignores the rest of the topic. The skill is detection — for hallucinated sources you verify cited URLs resolve and contain the claim, for premature finishing you check every sub-question was addressed, for tunnel vision you look at the spread of queries. Pick one of those three failure modes and walk me through exactly how you'd catch it automatically in production.

There are two broad strategies for how an agent thinks, and choosing wrong makes things harder than they need to be. A ReAct agent interleaves reasoning and action one step at a time — it thinks, takes an action, sees the result, then decides the next step, reacting as it goes. A planning agent instead drafts a full plan up front — list all the steps — then executes them in order. ReAct shines when the path is unpredictable and each result reshapes the next move; planning shines when the task decomposes cleanly into known steps and you want predictability and parallelism. Give me a research task where the planning approach clearly wins, and explain what about that task makes ReAct the wrong fit.

Not deduplicating search results — if the agent searches the same query twice and reads the same URLs twice, you waste tokens and money. Track visited URLs.
Sending full page content to the model — a web page can be 50,000 characters. Send only the first 5,000 characters, or use a chunked approach with relevance filtering.
Not separating the research phase from the writing phase — some agents try to research and write simultaneously, producing inconsistent reports. Gather all sources first, then write.
Not logging tool call sequences — when an agent fails or produces a poor report, you need to see every search query and page it visited. Log everything.

weeks.title: Multi-step workflows and orchestration
weeks.context:
Multi-step workflows chain multiple AI calls, external API calls, database operations, and conditional logic together into a coherent pipeline. As automations grow more complex, you need orchestration — a way to manage state, handle failures at any step, and retry or route around errors without starting from scratch.

Orchestration patterns: sequential (A → B → C), parallel (A and B run simultaneously, then C waits for both), conditional (if A returns X, go to B, else go to C), and fan-out/fan-in (process N items in parallel, aggregate results). The right pattern depends on the task — sequential is simplest, parallel is fastest when steps are independent.

This week you build a multi-step content production workflow using Prefect (a Python orchestration framework) and compare it to building the same workflow manually. You also learn state management: how to track which steps have completed when a workflow is interrupted and needs to resume.

mastery_questions: When automations grow past a single script, you need an orchestrator — a tool that runs your steps reliably, retries failures, and shows you what happened. Prefect is one such tool, and its two core building blocks are tasks and flows. A task is a single unit of work, like 'fetch one invoice', and a flow is the function that ties tasks together into a pipeline, like 'fetch all invoices, extract data, write to the database'. Yes, a flow can call another flow — that's how you compose a big pipeline out of smaller reusable ones, called subflows. Walk me through how you'd split a 'process daily support tickets' automation into tasks and a flow, and point out one place a subflow would help.

Re-running expensive work you've already done is a quiet money-leak in AI pipelines, and task caching is Prefect's answer. Caching means Prefect stores a task's result keyed on its inputs, so if you run the flow again with the same inputs, it returns the saved result instead of re-executing. In an AI context this is huge: if a task sends a 50-page document to an LLM for summarization and that costs real tokens, caching means a re-run after a downstream failure doesn't pay for that summary twice. The judgement is knowing what's safe to cache — pure, deterministic-enough steps yes, anything that must always be fresh no. Tell me which steps in a document-processing flow you'd cache and which you'd never cache, and why.

A pattern you'll reach for constantly in automation is fan-out/fan-in: fan-out means splitting one job into many parallel pieces, and fan-in means collecting all those results back together. Say you have 20 contracts to analyze with an LLM — fanning out runs them concurrently instead of one-by-one, which is far faster, and fanning in gathers the 20 results into one report. But you can't blast all 20 at the API at once or you'll hit rate limits, so you set a concurrency limit, say 5 at a time, meaning at most five run in parallel while the rest wait their turn. Walk me through how you'd process those 20 contracts with a concurrency limit of 5, and tell me what specifically goes wrong without that limit.

Pipelines fail — APIs time out, networks blip — so the real question is what your orchestrator does when one task throws an error. In Prefect, by default a failed task fails its flow, but the whole point of using an orchestrator is that you can configure smarter behaviour: you set retries so the task automatically tries again a few times with a delay between attempts, which handles transient glitches gracefully. You decide per task — a flaky network call gets retries, but a task that would duplicate a payment should not blindly retry. Explain how you'd configure retry behaviour for a task that calls a sometimes-flaky LLM API, and name one task where automatic retries would be dangerous.

There's a whole landscape of orchestration tools and picking the right one signals you actually understand the tradeoffs. Prefect is Python-native and great when your team writes Python and wants code-first pipelines with good local development. Airflow is the older, heavier standard — powerful and battle-tested at large scale, but more setup and ceremony. n8n is a visual, no-code/low-code tool great for connecting SaaS apps with drag-and-drop when you don't want to write much code. Tell me which of the three you'd pick for a solo consultant automating a client's invoice workflow, and which you'd pick for a 50-person data team, and defend each choice.

weeks.title: RAG — retrieval augmented generation
weeks.context:
RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) is how you give an LLM access to a large knowledge base without putting all of it in the context window. Instead of feeding the model an entire documentation library, you embed the documents into vector representations, store them in a vector database, and at query time retrieve only the most relevant chunks — then send those chunks plus the user's question to the model.

RAG is the dominant pattern for enterprise AI applications: chatbots that answer questions from company documentation, support agents that reference product manuals, search systems that understand natural language. Understanding the full pipeline — chunking, embedding, storing, retrieving, reranking, prompting — lets you build and debug these systems from first principles.

The hardest part of RAG is not the retrieval — it is getting the chunking and retrieval quality right. A RAG system that retrieves the wrong chunks gives the model bad context, which produces confident-sounding but wrong answers. Chunk quality and retrieval quality are the primary levers for RAG accuracy.

from openai import OpenAI

import numpy as np

mastery_questions: RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation, and it solves a real problem: an LLM doesn't know your private documents and can't be retrained for every client. The trick is to retrieve relevant chunks of your documents and stuff them into the prompt so the model answers from them. There are two distinct phases people confuse. At indexing time — done once, ahead of any question — you split your documents into chunks, convert each chunk to a vector embedding, and store them. At query time — every time a user asks something — you embed the question, find the most similar chunks, and feed those plus the question to the model. Walk me through both phases for a company knowledge-base bot, and be clear about which work happens once versus on every single query.

The magic that makes retrieval work is the vector embedding, so let's make sure you really get it. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, produced by an embedding model, such that texts with similar meaning end up with similar numbers — close together in that numeric space. This is why similarity search works: when a user asks 'how do I reset my password', its embedding lands near the embedding of a help article about password resets even if they share no exact words, because they mean the same thing. Keyword search would miss that; semantic search catches it. Explain in your own words why 'car' and 'automobile' would retrieve each other under embeddings but not under plain keyword matching.

How you cut your documents into pieces — your chunking strategy — quietly decides whether RAG works or flops. Fixed-size chunking just slices every N characters or tokens regardless of meaning, which is simple but can chop a sentence or idea in half right at the boundary. Semantic chunking instead tries to break at natural boundaries — paragraphs, sections, topic shifts — so each chunk is a coherent thought. It matters because a chunk that's half one idea and half another retrieves poorly and confuses the model. Give me a document type where fixed-size chunking is good enough, and one where you'd insist on semantic chunking, and explain what breaks if you get it wrong.

Basic similarity search is fast but blunt — it sometimes ranks a loosely-related chunk above the truly best one. Reranking is a second pass that fixes this: you retrieve a generous batch of candidate chunks with cheap similarity search, then a more powerful reranker model scores each candidate against the actual question and reorders them, so the best chunks rise to the top before you send them to the LLM. It costs extra time and money, so you use it when retrieval quality is the bottleneck and a wrong top chunk leads to a wrong answer. Walk me through when adding a reranker would noticeably improve a RAG system, and when it would just be wasted cost.

RAG can fail in ways that look like the model 'being dumb' but are actually retrieval problems, and diagnosing that is a core skill. The classic failure modes are: retrieval miss, where the right chunk simply wasn't fetched so the model never saw the answer; and good retrieval but bad generation, where the right chunk was there but the model ignored or misread it. To tell them apart you evaluate the two stages separately — check whether the correct chunk was in what you retrieved, then check whether the answer used it. Describe how you'd set up an evaluation that tells you whether a wrong RAG answer was caused by bad retrieval or bad generation, because the fix is completely different for each.
